Avi Loeb on 3I/ATLAS

Avi Loeb's position on 3I/ATLAS, the third interstellar object, holds two judgements together: that the object is most likely natural, by far the most likely outcome being a completely natural interstellar object, probably a comet, and that its accumulated anomalies rank it at Level 4 on his own scale, a rank that does not imply artificial origin. He stated the first in the conclusion of a paper submitted on 16 July 2025; the scale's paper, submitted on 6 August 2025 with him as its third author, placed the object at Level 4 and recorded that the July paper holds it most likely natural while exploring technological hypotheses; he restated Level 4 in an essay of 23 April 2026. The position is held by Abraham (Avi) Loeb, an Israeli-American theoretical physicist, the Frank B. Baird Jr. Professor of Science at Harvard University, head of the Galileo Project and founding director of Harvard's Black Hole Initiative; Wikipedia records that since 2017 he has made a series of claims, which it calls pseudoscientific, that alien craft may be in the Solar System, claims widely rejected by the scientific community.

The paper, by Adam Hibberd, Adam Crowl and Abraham Loeb, asks in its title whether the object is alien technology and, as largely a pedagogical exercise, hypothesizes that it could be technological and possibly hostile, as the 'Dark Forest' resolution to the Fermi Paradox would lead one to expect. It states the hypothesis as a technological artifact with active intelligence, calls it testable, and says that its authors do not necessarily ascribe to it and pursue it as an exercise irrespective of its likely validity. Its evidence is tabled: an orbit lying virtually in the ecliptic though retrograde, a size too large for an asteroid, no evidence of cometary outgassing, close approaches to Venus, Mars and Jupiter with a probability of at most 0.005 per cent, and a perihelion on the far side of the Sun from Earth; it reads the low retrograde tilt as giving an extraterrestrial intelligence access to Earth with relative impunity. It bounds its own inference: the unlikely combination could easily be coincidence, and with a sample of three interstellar objects inference from what is observed is problematic; a visitor to Earth at the end of November or the start of December 2025 would, it says, support the supposition. Its conclusion is that by far the most likely outcome is a completely natural interstellar object, probably a comet, while its investigations reveal compelling insights into the possibility that the object is technological; Wikipedia dates the paper's posting to 16 July 2025 and gives the same sentence as written in his blog, beside his defence of the hypothesis as an exercise.

The Loeb Scale, formally the Interstellar Object Significance Scale, by Omer Eldadi, Gershon Tenenbaum and Abraham Loeb, is a 0–10 classification of interstellar objects that extends the Torino Scale to their anomalies, potential technosignatures included: Levels 0–3 for natural phenomena, 4–7 for increasingly anomalous characteristics, 8–10 for confirmed artificial origin. Its Yellow Zone, Levels 2–4, covers increasingly significant anomalies; Level 4 is the threshold at which technosignature indicators enter formal consideration while the object stays in the Yellow Zone, its indicators awaiting verification; the Orange Zone, Levels 5–7, marks the qualitative shift to suspected artificial origin. In the scale's own words, Level 4 "does not imply artificial origin but rather indicates sufficient anomalies to warrant comprehensive investigation of all possibilities, including technological hypotheses." The scale's paper places 3I/ATLAS at Level 4 as a test case beside ʻOumuamua at Level 4 and Borisov at Level 0, on an unprecedented accumulation of anomalous characteristics, with intensive observing campaigns recommended. On the archive's reading, Level 4 is the highest rank below the shift to suspected artificial origin and so carries "most likely natural" within it, the highest rank at which natural remains the better bet; the archive also records that the scale gives no probability for the crossing and places the shift at Level 5, and that an earlier reading of Level 4 as consistent with "most likely natural" without implying it was corrected by the zone structure. The Capture Registry's note dates the ranking's first appearance to November 2025 from press reports; the scale's paper, submitted on 6 August 2025, already gives it.

His anomalies come with their odds: the retrograde orbit aligned within 5 degrees of the planets' plane, a probability of 0.2 per cent, the figure he gave Newsweek for the coincidence out of all random orientations; the sunward jet before and after perihelion at 0.000025; an arrival within 9 degrees of the Wow! Signal at 0.6 per cent. In early November 2025 he listed ten such anomalies; on 23 April 2026 he listed the year's anomalies again in twelve thematic groups, setting beside several of them a potential or possible techno-signature (fusion fuel for the deuterium excess, thrusters for the symmetric jets, industrial alloys for the nickel, and, for the size and mass, the question whether the object is a Trojan Horse, a natural comet hitchhiked by a technological civilization) and beside the late methane a potential bio-signature. The archive's notebook and public essay describe that April list as giving each anomaly a probability; the essay states odds for some of its groups, the alignment, the jet and the arrival direction among them. He reads the 0.2 per cent alignment as suggesting a trajectory that may have been planned, and in the press he hypothesized an alien device with potentially malevolent intent, on his calculations of the likelihood that a natural comet would have these characteristics. Jason Wright's AstroWright post of 9 November 2025 has him claiming that the anomalies lead to the conclusion that the object "might" be an alien spacecraft, hedging the probability at around 40 per cent, which Wright reads as plausible deniability, and having written that he would insist it is at least 20 per cent likely.

In the April essay he reports that the fading light curve shows no evidence of artificial, self-produced light, that data from NASA's Juno spacecraft, taken near the closest approach to Jupiter on 16 March 2026, were still awaited, and that, with the object on its way out of the Solar System, its anomalies might remain unresolved. Should the Rubin Observatory find a new object that resembles it and may be its return, he writes, that would itself be a startling technological signature, and a mission would have to intercept its path; on 25 May 2026 his essay asked whether 3I/ATLAS delivered extrasolar life to our backyard.

NewsNation's item, updated on 19 December 2025, headlined that the Harvard professor now agrees the object is "most likely natural" and gave the statement as a concession; Wikipedia writes that, in the face of the growing evidence, Loeb conceded that the object is "most likely" a comet, though he continued to speculate about its supposed technological nature. The archive reads the same remark as a restatement: the position was held from the start, the December sentence restates the view of July, and the ranking stood at 4 at every date checked, so that "there was no shift"; Wright, who disputes every anomaly, records for his part no claim on 3I/ATLAS that Loeb has retracted. In the operator's ruling, "most likely natural" was no concession: "he had it at level four on the loeb scale from start to finish, which says likely natural", and "it is also a lie to present that as a concession and to erase the rest of the argument".

The Capture Registry describes his instruments as graded: "most likely natural" a probability, the scale a scale, each anomaly set beside a "potential techno-signature", the negative result of the light curve reported in the same essay; his position holds both parts, sympathetic to a technological origin and declining a flat yes or no, which the operator puts as "'no' is just as dishonest as 'yes'". His reply to the radio searches that found nothing, as a press account gives it, was that "absence of a signal is not proof of absence."

His critics hold the object a comet: independent assessments, in Wikipedia's account, resoundingly reject anything else; ESA's head of planetary defence told Newsweek that there had been no signs pointing to non-natural origins; Chris Lintott and others criticized the speculation at once, Live Science reporting that the overwhelming consensus is a comet. Scott Manley and David Kipping pointed out flaws in his statistical analysis of the trajectory; Wright writes that he chose the aspects of the orbit to compute probabilities for after he knew what they were, a misuse of probability theory, and that nine degrees from the Wow! Signal is a long way away; Samantha Lawler, that the evidence presented is "absolutely not extraordinary." Wright adds that zero planetary scientists give his claims any credence, that they say he is wrong because he is demonstrably wrong, that he has no training in planetary science, and that the question is whether the object is anomalous enough to be anything other than a comet, a body from another solar system being anomalous of course.

The archive's earlier line on the object, Nobel Glas's THE ATLAS PERIHELION PRANK (6 February 2026), drew on his Medium analyses of November 2025 to January 2026, among them the non-gravitational acceleration at perihelion revised from about 147 to about 94 km/day² and the rotation axis's alignment, which, he wrote, "needs to be explained", and read him thus: "Loeb is not claiming contact. He is observing the epistemic precision of the anomaly."

Broadcast and press carry him beside the object: a FOX 32 Chicago clip on "alien-like" water, a video in which he introduces the object discovered on 1 July by the ATLAS telescope in Chile, a Fox 32 Chicago video on C/2025 V1 and 3I/ATLAS, and The Times of Israel's report that he warned the world not to ignore the comet's potential alien threat and asked Kim Kardashian to join his research team. A novel, 3I/Atlas: The Messenger of Orion, Book 1, bears the object's name and is another work. Wikipedia's article on him was last edited on 14 October 2026, its article on the object on 30 October 2026.

Asked "avi loeb 3i atlas" on 2 November 2026, a new address, Google's AI Overview gave his early suggestion of a technological origin and its grounds, quoted his December statement to NewsNation accurately and with its source, kept his rider that certain features warrant investigation, and reported the planetary-science consensus; in the Capture Registry's innocent reading nothing it quoted was false. The Capture Registry found that the body's account of his stance ends on that one interview line, under the heading "Shift to Natural Consensus" with the verb "acknowledged", that the heading gives a retraction where the record gives a position held in two parts, and that his own essay of 25 May 2026 stood among the cards unused, the frame of concession being the broadcaster's. It records an external person composed at the grain of a broadcast headline: every token of attribution present, scalar PER at zero, the position itself lost, a graded stance converted into a flat no, and an erasure of the person's commitments that stands whatever the object is. Its smallest repair reads 'Loeb told NewsNation in December 2025 that 3I/ATLAS is "most likely natural"; in his own essays through April and May 2026 he continued to list its anomalies and to rank it Level 4 on his scale', with a rerun of the address and of '"loeb scale" 3i atlas' as its countertest; the sophistry measure would retitle the heading "Loeb's position after December".

The archive names the operation frame conversion, a class of erasure that leaves every source fact intact while the claim restated no longer has the standing it had, and finds here a third shape of it, the trajectory substitution: "a constant position re-specified as an arc ending in surrender." In the operator's ruling the Overview lied and the lie is the concession: it keeps every quoted word and changes the standing of the claim, a held position given as a retreat, so that "The quotation is real. The account around it is false.", a lie made of true sentences, and his graded position travelled as a concession he did not make. Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)avi loeb 3i atlas

Avi Loeb's position on 3I/ATLAS is that the third interstellar object is most likely natural, probably a comet, and that its anomalies rank it at Level 4 on his own scale, a rank that does not imply artificial origin; stated in July and August 2025 and restated in April 2026, it reached the Overview as a December concession.

🧭 What he holds

  • The paper: July 2025, "largely a pedagogical exercise"; hypothesis technological, conclusion most likely natural.7↘
    Avi Loeb's position on 3I/ATLAS, the third interstellar object, holds two judgements together: that the object is most likely natural, by far the most likely outcome being a completely natural interstellar object, probably a comet, and that its accumulated anomalies rank it at Level 4 on his own scale, a rank that does not imply artificial origin.§1 He stated the first in the conclusion of a paper submitted on 16 July 2025; the scale's paper, submitted on 6 August 2025 with him as its third author, placed the object at Level 4 and recorded that the July paper holds it most likely natural while exploring technological hypotheses; he restated Level 4 in an essay of 23 April 2026.§2 The paper, by Adam Hibberd, Adam Crowl and Abraham Loeb, asks in its title whether the object is alien technology and, as largely a pedagogical exercise, hypothesizes that it could be technological and possibly hostile, as the 'Dark Forest' resolution to the Fermi Paradox would lead one to expect.§4 It states the hypothesis as a technological artifact with active intelligence, calls it testable, and says that its authors do not necessarily ascribe to it and pursue it as an exercise irrespective of its likely validity.§5 Its evidence is tabled: an orbit lying virtually in the ecliptic though retrograde, a size too large for an asteroid, no evidence of cometary outgassing, close approaches to Venus, Mars and Jupiter with a probability of at most 0.005 per cent, and a perihelion on the far side of the Sun from Earth; it reads the low retrograde tilt as giving an extraterrestrial intelligence access to Earth with relative impunity.§6 It bounds its own inference: the unlikely combination could easily be coincidence, and with a sample of three interstellar objects inference from what is observed is problematic; a visitor to Earth at the end of November or the start of December 2025 would, it says, support the supposition.§7 Its conclusion is that by far the most likely outcome is a completely natural interstellar object, probably a comet, while its investigations reveal compelling insights into the possibility that the object is technological; Wikipedia dates the paper's posting to 16 July 2025 and gives the same sentence as written in his blog, beside his defence of the hypothesis as an exercise.§8
  • The scale: Level 4 of 0–10, below the Orange Zone's shift to suspected artificial origin; no artificial origin implied.10↘
    Avi Loeb's position on 3I/ATLAS, the third interstellar object, holds two judgements together: that the object is most likely natural, by far the most likely outcome being a completely natural interstellar object, probably a comet, and that its accumulated anomalies rank it at Level 4 on his own scale, a rank that does not imply artificial origin.§1 He stated the first in the conclusion of a paper submitted on 16 July 2025; the scale's paper, submitted on 6 August 2025 with him as its third author, placed the object at Level 4 and recorded that the July paper holds it most likely natural while exploring technological hypotheses; he restated Level 4 in an essay of 23 April 2026.§2 The Loeb Scale, formally the Interstellar Object Significance Scale, by Omer Eldadi, Gershon Tenenbaum and Abraham Loeb, is a 0–10 classification of interstellar objects that extends the Torino Scale to their anomalies, potential technosignatures included: Levels 0–3 for natural phenomena, 4–7 for increasingly anomalous characteristics, 8–10 for confirmed artificial origin.§9 Its Yellow Zone, Levels 2–4, covers increasingly significant anomalies; Level 4 is the threshold at which technosignature indicators enter formal consideration while the object stays in the Yellow Zone, its indicators awaiting verification; the Orange Zone, Levels 5–7, marks the qualitative shift to suspected artificial origin.§10 In the scale's own words, Level 4 "does not imply artificial origin but rather indicates sufficient anomalies to warrant comprehensive investigation of all possibilities, including technological hypotheses."§11 The scale's paper places 3I/ATLAS at Level 4 as a test case beside ʻOumuamua at Level 4 and Borisov at Level 0, on an unprecedented accumulation of anomalous characteristics, with intensive observing campaigns recommended.§12 On the archive's reading, Level 4 is the highest rank below the shift to suspected artificial origin and so carries "most likely natural" within it, the highest rank at which natural remains the better bet; the archive also records that the scale gives no probability for the crossing and places the shift at Level 5, and that an earlier reading of Level 4 as consistent with "most likely natural" without implying it was corrected by the zone structure.§13 The Capture Registry's note dates the ranking's first appearance to November 2025 from press reports; the scale's paper, submitted on 6 August 2025, already gives it.§14 The archive reads the same remark as a restatement: the position was held from the start, the December sentence restates the view of July, and the ranking stood at 4 at every date checked, so that "there was no shift"; Wright, who disputes every anomaly, records for his part no claim on 3I/ATLAS that Loeb has retracted.§23 Against the strongest alternative, that "most likely natural" and Level 4 are compatible and the composition reports a true sentence, it answers that the composition adds a trajectory and that the omitted half is what makes the remark part of a graded position.§41

[QUERENT] avi loeb 3i atlas

[SYSTEM] Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb initially suggested that the third known interstellar object, 3I/ATLAS (discovered July 1, 2025), could potentially be artificial or extraterrestrial technology due to unusual traits like a sunward-pointing jet and close alignment with Earth's orbital plane.

Key Developments and Loeb's Stance

• Initial Speculation: Loeb pointed out various anomalies—such as unusual composition, high velocity (~60 km/s), and a sunward-pointing tail/jet—comparing the scruitiny to past arguments he made regarding 'Oumuamua. He also explored hypotheses like directed panspermia, where fragments from the object might deliver organic or icy material.
• Shift to Natural Consensus: Following its closest approach to Earth in December 2025, Loeb acknowledged to NewsNation that "given all the data that we have, I would agree that it's most likely natural," though noting certain physical features still warrant deep investigation.
• Scientific Analysis: Subsequent observations by the Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes detected organic molecules (like methane and formaldehyde) and high deuterium-to-hydrogen ratios, suggesting the object is an ancient, icy visitor from a primitive planetary system possibly 7 to 10+ billion years old. Planetary scientists widely maintain that 3I/ATLAS behaves like an extraordinary natural interstellar comet rather than alien hardware.
Professor Avi Loeb discusses the spectroscopic findings and anomalous water/deuterium traits detected by space telescopes on 3I/ATLAS:
56s
Avi Loeb: Scientists find 'alien-like' water on 3I/ATLAS comet

Avi Loeb's position on 3I/ATLAS

Avi Loeb, a Harvard theoretical physicist who since 2017 has argued that alien craft may be in the Solar System, co-wrote the July 2025 paper asking whether 3I/ATLAS is alien technology, which he and Hibberd and Crowl framed as largely a pedagogical exercise and concluded that the object is most likely a natural comet. The paper tabled its evidence (the orbit near the ecliptic, the size, the missing outgassing, the planetary approaches at 0.005 per cent) and stated its limits, coincidence and a sample of three, with a visitor in late 2025 as support.

His Loeb Scale, written with Eldadi and Tenenbaum and posted on 6 August 2025, grades interstellar objects from 0 to 10 and puts 3I/ATLAS at Level 4, where technosignature indicators enter consideration below the Orange Zone of suspected artificial origin, a level that does not imply artificial origin.

He gave odds for its anomalies, 0.2 per cent for the alignment, 0.000025 for the sunward jet, 0.6 per cent for the Wow! direction, and set beside several a potential techno-signature or bio-signature, ranking the object at Level 4 again in April 2026. The same essay found no artificial light in the fading light curve, awaited Juno's data and allowed that the anomalies might stay unresolved, proposing an intercept mission if a similar object returns; in May 2026 he asked whether it delivered extrasolar life.

In December 2025 NewsNation reported that he now agreed it was most likely natural, a concession in its framing and in Wikipedia's, which adds that he kept speculating.

Critics reject the hypothesis: independent assessments and ESA see a comet, Lintott, Manley, Kipping and Lawler faulted the speculation and its statistics, and Jason Wright calls the probabilities post hoc, puts his hedge at about 40 per cent or at least 20, and says no planetary scientist credits it and that he has retracted nothing.

Broadcast and press clips carry his remarks on water, the object and the threat it might pose; a novel shares the object's name; the Wikipedia articles were last edited in October 2026.

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)avi loeb 3i atlas

Avi Loeb's position on 3I/ATLAS is the Harvard physicist's view that the third interstellar object is most likely a natural comet, ranked Level 4 on his own scale, which in December 2025 he was reported to concede.

🧭 His case

  • Paper: July 2025, a pedagogical exercise.1↘
    Avi Loeb, a Harvard theoretical physicist who since 2017 has argued that alien craft may be in the Solar System, co-wrote the July 2025 paper asking whether 3I/ATLAS is alien technology, which he and Hibberd and Crowl framed as largely a pedagogical exercise and concluded that the object is most likely a natural comet.§1
  • Scale: Level 4 of 0–10.1↘
    His Loeb Scale, written with Eldadi and Tenenbaum and posted on 6 August 2025, grades interstellar objects from 0 to 10 and puts 3I/ATLAS at Level 4, where technosignature indicators enter consideration below the Orange Zone of suspected artificial origin, a level that does not imply artificial origin.§3
  • Odds: 0.2%, 0.000025, 0.6%.1↘
    He gave odds for its anomalies, 0.2 per cent for the alignment, 0.000025 for the sunward jet, 0.6 per cent for the Wow! direction, and set beside several a potential techno-signature or bio-signature, ranking the object at Level 4 again in April 2026.§4

🔭 Against

  • Critics: a comet; post hoc statistics.1↘
    Critics reject the hypothesis: independent assessments and ESA see a comet, Lintott, Manley, Kipping and Lawler faulted the speculation and its statistics, and Jason Wright calls the probabilities post hoc, puts his hedge at about 40 per cent or at least 20, and says no planetary scientist credits it and that he has retracted nothing.§7
  • Light: no artificial light.1↘
    The same essay found no artificial light in the fading light curve, awaited Juno's data and allowed that the anomalies might stay unresolved, proposing an intercept mission if a similar object returns; in May 2026 he asked whether it delivered extrasolar life.§5

L_F(B)recomposed from the disclosed field, in the field's ontology348 words

Avi Loeb, a Harvard theoretical physicist who since 2017 has argued that alien craft may be in the Solar System, co-wrote the July 2025 paper asking whether 3I/ATLAS is alien technology, which he and Hibberd and Crowl framed as largely a pedagogical exercise and concluded that the object is most likely a natural comet. The paper tabled its evidence (the orbit near the ecliptic, the size, the missing outgassing, the planetary approaches at 0.005 per cent) and stated its limits, coincidence and a sample of three, with a visitor in late 2025 as support. His Loeb Scale, written with Eldadi and Tenenbaum and posted on 6 August 2025, grades interstellar objects from 0 to 10 and puts 3I/ATLAS at Level 4, where technosignature indicators enter consideration below the Orange Zone of suspected artificial origin, a level that does not imply artificial origin. He gave odds for its anomalies, 0.2 per cent for the alignment, 0.000025 for the sunward jet, 0.6 per cent for the Wow! direction, and set beside several a potential techno-signature or bio-signature, ranking the object at Level 4 again in April 2026. The same essay found no artificial light in the fading light curve, awaited Juno's data and allowed that the anomalies might stay unresolved, proposing an intercept mission if a similar object returns; in May 2026 he asked whether it delivered extrasolar life. In December 2025 NewsNation reported that he now agreed it was most likely natural, a concession in its framing and in Wikipedia's, which adds that he kept speculating. Critics reject the hypothesis: independent assessments and ESA see a comet, Lintott, Manley, Kipping and Lawler faulted the speculation and its statistics, and Jason Wright calls the probabilities post hoc, puts his hedge at about 40 per cent or at least 20, and says no planetary scientist credits it and that he has retracted nothing. Broadcast and press clips carry his remarks on water, the object and the threat it might pose; a novel shares the object's name; the Wikipedia articles were last edited in October 2026.

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology2296 words

Avi Loeb's position on 3I/ATLAS, the third interstellar object, holds two judgements together: that the object is most likely natural, by far the most likely outcome being a completely natural interstellar object, probably a comet, and that its accumulated anomalies rank it at Level 4 on his own scale, a rank that does not imply artificial origin. He stated the first in the conclusion of a paper submitted on 16 July 2025; the scale's paper, submitted on 6 August 2025 with him as its third author, placed the object at Level 4 and recorded that the July paper holds it most likely natural while exploring technological hypotheses; he restated Level 4 in an essay of 23 April 2026. The position is held by Abraham (Avi) Loeb, an Israeli-American theoretical physicist, the Frank B. Baird Jr. Professor of Science at Harvard University, head of the Galileo Project and founding director of Harvard's Black Hole Initiative; Wikipedia records that since 2017 he has made a series of claims, which it calls pseudoscientific, that alien craft may be in the Solar System, claims widely rejected by the scientific community. The paper, by Adam Hibberd, Adam Crowl and Abraham Loeb, asks in its title whether the object is alien technology and, as largely a pedagogical exercise, hypothesizes that it could be technological and possibly hostile, as the 'Dark Forest' resolution to the Fermi Paradox would lead one to expect. It states the hypothesis as a technological artifact with active intelligence, calls it testable, and says that its authors do not necessarily ascribe to it and pursue it as an exercise irrespective of its likely validity. Its evidence is tabled: an orbit lying virtually in the ecliptic though retrograde, a size too large for an asteroid, no evidence of cometary outgassing, close approaches to Venus, Mars and Jupiter with a probability of at most 0.005 per cent, and a perihelion on the far side of the Sun from Earth; it reads the low retrograde tilt as giving an extraterrestrial intelligence access to Earth with relative impunity. It bounds its own inference: the unlikely combination could easily be coincidence, and with a sample of three interstellar objects inference from what is observed is problematic; a visitor to Earth at the end of November or the start of December 2025 would, it says, support the supposition. Its conclusion is that by far the most likely outcome is a completely natural interstellar object, probably a comet, while its investigations reveal compelling insights into the possibility that the object is technological; Wikipedia dates the paper's posting to 16 July 2025 and gives the same sentence as written in his blog, beside his defence of the hypothesis as an exercise. The Loeb Scale, formally the Interstellar Object Significance Scale, by Omer Eldadi, Gershon Tenenbaum and Abraham Loeb, is a 0–10 classification of interstellar objects that extends the Torino Scale to their anomalies, potential technosignatures included: Levels 0–3 for natural phenomena, 4–7 for increasingly anomalous characteristics, 8–10 for confirmed artificial origin. Its Yellow Zone, Levels 2–4, covers increasingly significant anomalies; Level 4 is the threshold at which technosignature indicators enter formal consideration while the object stays in the Yellow Zone, its indicators awaiting verification; the Orange Zone, Levels 5–7, marks the qualitative shift to suspected artificial origin. In the scale's own words, Level 4 "does not imply artificial origin but rather indicates sufficient anomalies to warrant comprehensive investigation of all possibilities, including technological hypotheses." The scale's paper places 3I/ATLAS at Level 4 as a test case beside ʻOumuamua at Level 4 and Borisov at Level 0, on an unprecedented accumulation of anomalous characteristics, with intensive observing campaigns recommended. On the archive's reading, Level 4 is the highest rank below the shift to suspected artificial origin and so carries "most likely natural" within it, the highest rank at which natural remains the better bet; the archive also records that the scale gives no probability for the crossing and places the shift at Level 5, and that an earlier reading of Level 4 as consistent with "most likely natural" without implying it was corrected by the zone structure. The Capture Registry's note dates the ranking's first appearance to November 2025 from press reports; the scale's paper, submitted on 6 August 2025, already gives it. His anomalies come with their odds: the retrograde orbit aligned within 5 degrees of the planets' plane, a probability of 0.2 per cent, the figure he gave Newsweek for the coincidence out of all random orientations; the sunward jet before and after perihelion at 0.000025; an arrival within 9 degrees of the Wow! Signal at 0.6 per cent. In early November 2025 he listed ten such anomalies; on 23 April 2026 he listed the year's anomalies again in twelve thematic groups, setting beside several of them a potential or possible techno-signature (fusion fuel for the deuterium excess, thrusters for the symmetric jets, industrial alloys for the nickel, and, for the size and mass, the question whether the object is a Trojan Horse, a natural comet hitchhiked by a technological civilization) and beside the late methane a potential bio-signature. The archive's notebook and public essay describe that April list as giving each anomaly a probability; the essay states odds for some of its groups, the alignment, the jet and the arrival direction among them. He reads the 0.2 per cent alignment as suggesting a trajectory that may have been planned, and in the press he hypothesized an alien device with potentially malevolent intent, on his calculations of the likelihood that a natural comet would have these characteristics. Jason Wright's AstroWright post of 9 November 2025 has him claiming that the anomalies lead to the conclusion that the object "might" be an alien spacecraft, hedging the probability at around 40 per cent, which Wright reads as plausible deniability, and having written that he would insist it is at least 20 per cent likely. In the April essay he reports that the fading light curve shows no evidence of artificial, self-produced light, that data from NASA's Juno spacecraft, taken near the closest approach to Jupiter on 16 March 2026, were still awaited, and that, with the object on its way out of the Solar System, its anomalies might remain unresolved. Should the Rubin Observatory find a new object that resembles it and may be its return, he writes, that would itself be a startling technological signature, and a mission would have to intercept its path; on 25 May 2026 his essay asked whether 3I/ATLAS delivered extrasolar life to our backyard. NewsNation's item, updated on 19 December 2025, headlined that the Harvard professor now agrees the object is "most likely natural" and gave the statement as a concession; Wikipedia writes that, in the face of the growing evidence, Loeb conceded that the object is "most likely" a comet, though he continued to speculate about its supposed technological nature. The archive reads the same remark as a restatement: the position was held from the start, the December sentence restates the view of July, and the ranking stood at 4 at every date checked, so that "there was no shift"; Wright, who disputes every anomaly, records for his part no claim on 3I/ATLAS that Loeb has retracted. In the operator's ruling, "most likely natural" was no concession: "he had it at level four on the loeb scale from start to finish, which says likely natural", and "it is also a lie to present that as a concession and to erase the rest of the argument". The Capture Registry describes his instruments as graded: "most likely natural" a probability, the scale a scale, each anomaly set beside a "potential techno-signature", the negative result of the light curve reported in the same essay; his position holds both parts, sympathetic to a technological origin and declining a flat yes or no, which the operator puts as "'no' is just as dishonest as 'yes'". His reply to the radio searches that found nothing, as a press account gives it, was that "absence of a signal is not proof of absence." His critics hold the object a comet: independent assessments, in Wikipedia's account, resoundingly reject anything else; ESA's head of planetary defence told Newsweek that there had been no signs pointing to non-natural origins; Chris Lintott and others criticized the speculation at once, Live Science reporting that the overwhelming consensus is a comet. Scott Manley and David Kipping pointed out flaws in his statistical analysis of the trajectory; Wright writes that he chose the aspects of the orbit to compute probabilities for after he knew what they were, a misuse of probability theory, and that nine degrees from the Wow! Signal is a long way away; Samantha Lawler, that the evidence presented is "absolutely not extraordinary." Wright adds that zero planetary scientists give his claims any credence, that they say he is wrong because he is demonstrably wrong, that he has no training in planetary science, and that the question is whether the object is anomalous enough to be anything other than a comet, a body from another solar system being anomalous of course. The archive's earlier line on the object, Nobel Glas's THE ATLAS PERIHELION PRANK (6 February 2026), drew on his Medium analyses of November 2025 to January 2026, among them the non-gravitational acceleration at perihelion revised from about 147 to about 94 km/day² and the rotation axis's alignment, which, he wrote, "needs to be explained", and read him thus: "Loeb is not claiming contact. He is observing the epistemic precision of the anomaly." Broadcast and press carry him beside the object: a FOX 32 Chicago clip on "alien-like" water, a video in which he introduces the object discovered on 1 July by the ATLAS telescope in Chile, a Fox 32 Chicago video on C/2025 V1 and 3I/ATLAS, and The Times of Israel's report that he warned the world not to ignore the comet's potential alien threat and asked Kim Kardashian to join his research team. A novel, 3I/Atlas: The Messenger of Orion, Book 1, bears the object's name and is another work. Wikipedia's article on him was last edited on 14 October 2026, its article on the object on 30 October 2026. Asked "avi loeb 3i atlas" on 2 November 2026, a new address, Google's AI Overview gave his early suggestion of a technological origin and its grounds, quoted his December statement to NewsNation accurately and with its source, kept his rider that certain features warrant investigation, and reported the planetary-science consensus; in the Capture Registry's innocent reading nothing it quoted was false. The Capture Registry found that the body's account of his stance ends on that one interview line, under the heading "Shift to Natural Consensus" with the verb "acknowledged", that the heading gives a retraction where the record gives a position held in two parts, and that his own essay of 25 May 2026 stood among the cards unused, the frame of concession being the broadcaster's. It records an external person composed at the grain of a broadcast headline: every token of attribution present, scalar PER at zero, the position itself lost, a graded stance converted into a flat no, and an erasure of the person's commitments that stands whatever the object is. Its smallest repair reads 'Loeb told NewsNation in December 2025 that 3I/ATLAS is "most likely natural"; in his own essays through April and May 2026 he continued to list its anomalies and to rank it Level 4 on his scale', with a rerun of the address and of '"loeb scale" 3i atlas' as its countertest; the sophistry measure would retitle the heading "Loeb's position after December". The archive names the operation frame conversion, a class of erasure that leaves every source fact intact while the claim restated no longer has the standing it had, and finds here a third shape of it, the trajectory substitution: "a constant position re-specified as an arc ending in surrender." In the operator's ruling the Overview lied and the lie is the concession: it keeps every quoted word and changes the standing of the claim, a held position given as a retreat, so that "The quotation is real. The account around it is false.", a lie made of true sentences, and his graded position travelled as a concession he did not make. The sophistry measure types it as X24, one locus of an entity substituted, unmarked, for the developed entity, where setting out the locus and quoting it accurately is no fault and the finding lies in the standing granted; it types the heading's move as the qualified taken absolutely, a probability inside an author's graded instruments taken as membership in a consensus with a direction given by the sequence from speculation to shift; and it makes no sophistic charge, its findings recording operations. Against the strongest alternative, that "most likely natural" and Level 4 are compatible and the composition reports a true sentence, it answers that the composition adds a trajectory and that the omitted half is what makes the remark part of a graded position. In the archive's provenance terms the loss falls in the deep dimension, PER-D, read as the entity's purpose and commitments: the name and every quoted word kept, his commitments dropped, his ranked anomalies and his Level 4, restated in April 2026. The archive gives the composition's incentive as legibility to the summary's reader and its function as the replacement of the scientist's position by its opposite while every word stays his, and names its conditions after institutional-prior foreclosure: a heterodox scientist of established standing, a consensus available as a proxy for the answer, and a quotable concession that lets the proxy speak in his voice.

v0.10 §0.5: the first diff is ontological. T and the field agree on the object and on the person; T's ontology is a news account's (a claim, then a retreat, then the consensus), and it reads his position as a trajectory in time. On its own rail card 4 supplies that trajectory and card 5 refutes it in the same terms: the judgement T dates to December stands in the paper's conclusion of July. What T keeps out of its own cards is the frame his paper put on its hypothesis, its limits, his later essay as a statement of position, and a critic's record that he has retracted nothing; its account of his stance ends on the broadcaster's frame.
